module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 541

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/541](https://www.erdosproblems.com/541)
- [ErSz76] Erdős, E. and Szemerédi, E., On a problem of Graham. Publ. Math. Debrecen (1976),
  123--127.
- [GHW10] Gao, Weidong and Hamidoune, Yahya Ould and Wang, Guoqing, Distinct length modular zero-sum
  subsequences: a proof of Graham's conjecture. J. Number Theory (2010), 1425--1431.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos541

/--
Let $a_1, \dots, a_p$ be (not necessarily distinct) residues modulo a prime $p$, such that there
exists some $r$ so that if $S \subseteq [p]$ is non-empty and
$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$$
then $|S| = r$.

Must there be at most two distinct residues amongst the $a_i$?

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos541.lean"]
theorem erdos_541 : answer(True) ↔ (∀ p, Fact p.Prime → ∀ (a : Fin p → ZMod p),
    (∃ r, ∀ (S : Finset (Fin p)), S ≠ ∅ → ∑ i ∈ S, a i = 0 → S.card = r) →
      (Set.range a).ncard ≤ 2) := by
  sorry

/-- Gao, Hamidoune, and Wang [GHW10] solved this for all moduli `p` (not necessarily prime). -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_541.variants.general_moduli (p : ℕ) (a : Fin p → ZMod p)
    (ha₀ : ∃ r, ∀ (S : Finset (Fin p)), S ≠ ∅ → ∑ i ∈ S, a i = 0 → S.card = r) :
      (Set.range a).ncard ≤ 2 := by
  sorry

/-- This was proved by Erdős and Szemerédi [ErSz76] for p sufficiently large. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_541.variants.large_primes : ∀ᶠ p in atTop, p.Prime → ∀ a : Fin p → ZMod p,
    (∃ r, ∀ (S : Finset (Fin p)), S ≠ ∅ → ∑ i ∈ S, a i = 0 → S.card = r) →
      (Set.range a).ncard ≤ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos541

reformulations.difference: The Lean quantifies over all residues a : Fin p → ZMod p, zero allowed. Graham's conjecture as proved by Erdős–Szemerédi assumes non-zero residues. GHW (arXiv 0902.4758) quote ES76 verbatim: "Let p be a prime and a_1, …, a_p p non-zero residues (mod p)". GHW's Theorem A states ES76 for integers in [1, p−1].
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Suppose some a_i = 0. Then {i} is a zero-sum set, so r = 1. A second zero a_j = 0 would give the zero-sum pair {i, j}, so a_i is the only zero. No non-empty subset T of the other p−1 indices is zero-sum, since otherwise T ∪ {i} would be zero-sum of size ≥ 2. A zero-sum-free sequence of length p−1 over Z_p is constant: its partial sums are exactly the p−1 non-zero residues, and swapping two adjacent distinct terms would change exactly one partial sum and repeat or hit 0. So the sequence is 0 followed by p−1 copies of some g, which has 2 distinct values. The zero-containing cases therefore satisfy the conclusion for every prime, and the Lean statement is equivalent to the non-zero version that ES76 proved. erdosproblems.com itself states the problem with arbitrary "(not necessarily distinct) residues". Brute force over all primes ≤ 7 with zeros allowed found no counterexample.

reformulations.difference: Like the erdosproblems.com statement, the right-hand side allows zero residues. Graham's original conjecture (ES76, quoted in GHW) speaks of p non-zero residues mod p.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same argument as for large_primes. A zero term forces r = 1 and exactly one zero. The remaining p−1 terms are zero-sum-free of maximal length, hence constant. So every zero-containing sequence has ≤ 2 distinct values, and the statement with zeros allowed is equivalent to the non-zero version. The Lean matches the cited erdosproblems.com text word for word on this point.

reformulations.difference: `p : ℕ` includes p = 0, where `ZMod 0 = ℤ`. GHW's Theorem 1.1 is for positive integers n. The hypothesis `∃ r, ∀ S ≠ ∅, ∑ i ∈ S, a i = 0 → S.card = r` is phrased differently from Grynkiewicz's "there is a unique r ∈ [1,n] with 0 ∈ Σ_r(S)".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For p = 0, `Fin 0` is empty, so `Set.range a = ∅` and the conclusion `0 ≤ 2` holds trivially. I proved this in scratch with `simp [Set.range_eq_empty]`, together with p = 1 and 2. For p ≥ 1 the statement is exactly GHW Theorem 1.1. The two hypothesis forms agree because any sequence of n elements of Z_n has a non-empty zero-sum subsequence: among the n prefix sums, one is 0 or two coincide. So "all zero-sum subsets have the same size" is the same as "there is a unique zero-sum length". The hypothesis is never vacuous.

review.notes:
No findings and no status issues. The file says research solved, answer(True), with formal_proof lean4. The source says 'PROVED (LEAN) — solved in the affirmative and the proof verified in Lean'; the teorth database says 'proved (Lean)'. The variants are solved by GHW10 and ES76.

Checks done in /workspace/review:
(1) #check/#print of all three statements: p : ℕ, sums in ZMod p, r : ℕ, and ∀ᶠ scoping over the whole implication.
(2) Brute force over all a : Fin n → ZMod n using the actual Finset/ZMod objects for n ≤ 5, and over sorted sequences for n ≤ 10. There is no counterexample to the general-moduli claim. The hypothesis is satisfiable for every n (2, 6, 10, 24, 20, 48, 44, 60, 72 multisets for n = 2..10), so nothing is vacuous.
(3) The boundary moduli p = 0, 1, 2 in general_moduli are proved trivially true in scratch.

Points considered and rejected as findings:
(a) The Lean docstring says 'residues modulo a prime p', while the current erdosproblems.com text says only 'residues modulo p'. The page's own remark (ES76 'for p sufficiently large'; GHW 'for all moduli (not necessarily prime)') and Bloom's forum comment show p is meant to be prime. The file states the all-moduli version separately as general_moduli, and the answer is True under either reading.
(b) The existential hypothesis could hold vacuously if no zero-sum subset existed. But a length-n sequence over Z_n always has one, and vacuity would in any case only strengthen the claim.
(c) The module docstring's reference 'Erdős, E.' (should be P. Erdős) is copied from the erdosproblems.com bibliography. It is a harmless citation slip and not reported.

I did not read ES76 itself. I relied on GHW's verbatim quotation of its conjecture statement and GHW's Theorem A, and Grynkiewicz's abstract gives the same account.
